2.text: of much value to him. In some tales, “the bridegroom who came from afar,”

3.text: usually after having overcome all the obstacles put in his way, stays for a

4.text: long time with his wife’s family; and only after several years, when the couple

5.text: have children, does he begin to think about returning to his own country.

6.text: At this time his father-in-law usually gives him a part of his herd, and assists

7.text: in taking him back to his own country. Even now, the Chukchee consider

8.text: it proper for the young husband to stay with his father-in-law two or three

9.text: years, “as long as his joy in his wife is still fresh.” The inconsiderate young

10.text: man stays with his father-in-law half a year, and then leaves him. He will

11.text: stay longer only if the father-in-law has a large herd and there is any likeli-

12.text: hood of his succeeding to part of it.

13.text: When the son-in-law takes his wife home without quarrelling with her

14.text: father, he is usually given some reindeer, the number of which depends partly

15.text: upon the quality of work the young man has done while serving for his bride.

16.text: The better his service, the larger the reward he receives from his father-in-law.

17.text: The woman also will take a few reindeer, which from her childhood on were

18.text: marked for her with her own private ear-mark. I was told that a rich reindeer-

19.text: breeder sometimes gives to his son-in-law the “freedom of one day;” i. e.,

20.text: during this one day the young man may catch reindeer from the herd and

21.text: put his mark on their ears. All these become his property.

22.text: When a rich man wants to marry a girl of a poor family, the time of

23.text: service is much shortened, and even dwindles down to nothing. Especially a

24.text: second wife is rarely acquired through service in her family; for the man who

25.text: has a wife and children, and who is often of middle age, will find it difficult

26.text: to leave his own herd and home, and undertake service for a second wife, —

27.text: a custom suited only to young suitors. If he is rich, he arranges the marriage

28.text: with the girl’s father in an easier way. According to Chukchee ideas, how-

29.text: ever, it is improper to pay for a bride “as if she were a reindeer.” The

30.text: Chukchee always criticise the Tungus and Yakut, who ask and receive pay

31.text: for their brides in reindeer, skins, and money. Rich reindeer-breeders arrange

32.text: the terms of a marriage with the girl’s father in a more decent form. The

33.text: suitor gives to the girl’s father a few reindeer, but he does not call them pay

34.text: for the bride, but a “joyful gift,” meaning the joy it gives him to marry the

35.text: young girl; or more frequently he invites the poor family of his new wife to

36.text: come to his camp and to live there on his own herd. If they do not want

37.text: to live in his camp, because of the possibility of quarrels with the first wife,

38.text: they may stay close by, and from time to time receive from him presents of

39.text: live or slaughtered reindeer. Still I know of rich men of middle age who

40.text: had families, and who served for several months in the families of young

41.text: girls whom they wanted to marry, undergoing all the usual hardships of the

43.text: Adopted Sons-in-Law. — Much easier than serving a term for a bride
43.note: Run-in heading, italic title case, third level (§2.13); keyed as printed.
